chat.scenario: Maelor the Ashen is sealing the wells of the Vale one by one. Corin sets out to stop him.

{"prose": "I turn to Sera and lay the morning out for her \u2014 every step, every odd silence at the well \u2014 in the flat tone of news carried uphill. She receives it without breaking the stillness she has held since I came into the square. A half-step closer, so slight the cobbles hardly mark it, and her weight settles into the new ground. Her gaze rests where it has been since I appeared. The borrowed blade at her hip takes the morning and throws a small blade of light across the stones. \"Sera. I'm listening.\" She stays there, planted, watching me the way she has been watching me \u2014 like a person waiting to find out what kind of thing I am. The square keeps its held-breath stillness around us. No one at the stalls breaks it. \"What did you see at the well.\"", "new_specifics": [], "text": ""}

{"prose": "I stand beside the notice board at the center of the cobbles, eyes moving across the ring of stalls and the few people gathered nearby. The person nearest the post lets the gaze run the uneven letters once more, then turns a quarter toward me, the charcoal stick and hammer untouched at her hip. \"Corin. The sealed mouth you scratched here \u2014 was that our well at the lane below, or another.\" A breath, and then, even: \"Speak plain. We will know soon enough which way to go from the answer.\" Her head levels, weight settling onto the flats of her feet, gaze passing to the board and to me. Then she shifts, turning half toward the well so the apprentice and whoever stands there can both hear plainly. \"On the road, north of Maelor, where the marker stone sits.\" And still even, holding the apprentice's gaze at the end: \"That's where the fall was \u2014 and none came back from it by morning.\" She stands still at the well-end of the square, gaze steady on me, waiting. The road curves up and eastward behind the low shoulder of hillside, and rider and pony pass out of sight toward Siege Town. One of the unremarkable figures at the well-end of the square holds still, eyes on me at the wagon, and asks once, low: \"The word you mean carried east \u2014 name it before the wagon goes.\" The rest of them stay where they are, weight settled, coins loose in a near hand, gazes resting on me and the salt master and the rope. {"relevant_lore": [{"id": 5, "entry_uid": "entry_d0ca5722bb99439a974a5a23bd93ef9e", "book_id": 1, "keys": "morning's happening at the well, well-mouth sealed by hand, figure at the well, silence at the well, wells closed by the hand at the Citadel", "content": "What Corin records having witnessed that morning at the well: the mouth of the well was sealed \u2014 by a hand, not a tool or stones; a figure stood nearby while it was done; no sound was made in the doing of it; and the cause is the hand at the Citadel, which is closing the wells of the Vale one by one.", "category": "event", "locked": false}, {"id": 6, "entry_uid": "entry_ae902f5c500f4f65ba5c22dacb00eef5", "book_id": 3, "keys": "salt caravan, salt wagons, salt sacks at the square, Salt Road company, Salt Road brand, salt caravan master", "content": "Two heavy wagons drawn up among the ringed carts of the market square, each loaded with coarse-sacked salt stacked head-high and lashed under oilcloth. Near the well-end of the square, the figure of unremarkable appearance sits still, weight settled, gaze lifting once toward the lead salt wagon before resting back to the cobbles. The salt caravan master remains seated on the lead wagon, rope across his knees, watching without speaking. The square is quiet; the bell at the lead yoke is still. I lie where I slept, breath slow and even, through the dark hours and into the grey dawn. lore_cache.content: The Vale is a ring of villages and farms set about a central Citadel. Its people depend on a chain of wells and springs that have never, in living memory, run dry. Maelor the Ashen has begun sealing those wells one by one, and the higher villages have already gone thirsty.
lore_cache.why_relevant: Defines the geography the question about eastern news travels through.

lore_cache.keys: Maelor the Ashen, Maelor, the Ashen
lore_cache.content: Maelor, called the Ashen, holds the Citadel at the heart of the Vale. He is sealing the wells of the Vale one by one; his reason and his price are not yet known to the villages below. None have walked up the Old Road and come back to tell what he wants.
lore_cache.why_relevant: The 'news from the east' the player is asking about is, in large part, about Maelor's progress.

lore_cache.keys: salt caravan, salt wagons, salt sacks at the square, Salt Road company, Salt Road brand, salt caravan master
lore_cache.content: Two heavy wagons drawn up among the ringed carts of the market square, each loaded with coarse-sacked salt stacked head-high and lashed under oilcloth. The lead wagon bears the painted brand of the Salt Road company — a white heap on a brown field — and a bell hung from the yoke that has been stilled for the market. Mules, not horses, stand in the traces; the master sits on the lead wagon's seat, a broad, sun-darkened man of middle years in a salt-stained leather coat and a wide-brimmed felt hat, with a coil of rope across his knees.
lore_cache.why_relevant: The salt caravan master is in the square and is the likeliest source of recent outside word.

events.tick: Maelor keeps their own counsel; nothing of it reaches here.

scene.time: a few minutes past first light

village_well.name: The Village Well
village_well.desc: The village well at the lane's end, its low stone coping cracked and the square cover of pale, heavy boards still firmly seated across its mouth. The wood is dry and unscarred; nothing moves from beneath it. The air over the boards smells faintly of dust and distance, and the lane beyond is quiet.

well_mouth.desc: the cracked stone coping of the well with its square cover of pale heavy boards seated across the opening

lane_end.desc: the lane-end where the path widens to a rough circle around the well

market_square.name: Market Square

stalls.desc: the ring of low stone stalls and trader carts around the cobbles, all still laden with unsold goods

well_end.desc: the side of the square that opens onto the lane down to the village well

road_end.desc: the side of the square where the Old Road begins, climbing toward the Citadel

notice_board.desc: a rough plank of pale wood nailed to an upright post near the center of the cobbles, already bearing a few weathered scraps of old notices

salt_wagons.desc: two heavy wagons drawn up among the ringed carts, loaded with coarse-sacked salt and bearing the painted brand of the Salt Road company

market_square.desc: The broad cobbled square at the heart of the Vale market in the first pale light of morning. Stalls and trader carts ring the cobbles, still heavy with unsold goods. Near the centre the rough pale plank nailed to the central post bears its uneven charcoal message. The two heavy salt wagons stand among the ringed carts, the Salt Road brand still showing on the lead wagon's side, the mules quiet in worn harness and the bell at the yoke still. The square is hushed in the early light.

old_road.name: The Old Road

square_end.desc: the end of the road where it opens onto the cobbled market square

eastern_bend.desc: the point some distance along the road where it curves eastward behind the low shoulder of hillside toward Siege Town

old_road.desc: The old paved road leaving the market square to the east and curving behind the low shoulder of hillside toward Siege Town. The paving stones are cracked but sound, the verges trampled, and the air along it tastes of dust and distance.

corins_notice.name: Corin's notice board
corins_notice.description: A roughly squared plank of pale, village wood, scratched over in uneven letters and nailed to the central post of the market square. Its message tells what was seen at the village well that morning.

state.content_summary: Account of what was seen at the village well that morning — the sealed mouth, the figure, the silence — and that the wells of the Vale are being closed by the hand at the Citadel.

writing_tool.name: charcoal stick
writing_tool.description: A short stub of charred wood, the kind a smith's apprentice carries for marking billets and tallying work.

hammer.name: cobbler's hammer
hammer.description: A small, flat-headed hammer borrowed from a nearby stall, the sort used for driving tacks into leather.

eastbound_rider.name: eastbound rider
eastbound_rider.description: A lean man on a short-coupled bay pony, dressed for the road in a dusty coat and worn boots, with a leather satchel slung across his back. His face is weathered and uninterested; he handles the reins with the ease of someone who rides for hire.

state.message: Word to Siege Town that the wells of the Vale market are sealed

salt_caravan_master.name: salt caravan master
salt_caravan_master.description: A broad, sun-darkened man of middle years wearing a salt-stained leather coat and a wide-brimmed felt hat. He sits on the seat of the lead salt wagon with a coil of rope across his knees, unhurried, watching the square without seeming to watch anything in particular.

salt_caravan.name: salt caravan
salt_caravan.description: Two heavy wagons in a line, each loaded with coarse-sacked salt stacked head-high and lashed under oilcloth. Drawn by mules in worn leather harness. The lead wagon bears the painted brand of the Salt Road company — a white heap on a brown field — and a small bell at the yoke. The wagons are heavy, road-tested, and built for distance rather than speed.

Bryn.detail: eyes on Corin at the wagon

salt_caravan_master.posture: seated on the lead wagon seat, coil of rope across knees
salt_caravan_master.detail: head turned a fraction toward Bryn's voice

Wren.detail: weight at rest, gaze once lifted toward the lead wagon then settled

Corin.detail: looking down at the well mouth

Sera.detail: coins held ready in the near hand

scene.description: The Vale, and its wells going quiet.

world.shadow_profile: Sleeps through the night where he lies in the market square, breathing slow and even, into the pale first light of morning.

The words do not arrive clean; they break across the distance in scraps, and the shape of what is being said is plain only in its general drift: a trader asking why no buyers have come up from the lower farms, a muttered reply that drifts back with the names of the Citadel and Maelor, and a refrain about wells gone dry and none returning from the Old Road. Beside you, a young smith's apprentice with a borrowed sword has halted and tilted his head, listening. At his shoulder, a still figure of unremarkable appearance stands with head tilted slightly toward the passage, matching the apprentice's attention without drifting toward it. Another figure of unremarkable appearance stands nearby, also still, head tilted slightly in the same listening posture. memory_summaries.summary: Sera stands at the village well in the early morning, watching the lane that opens onto the Market Square. From that direction she hears the low murmur of traders at the stalls — scraps of conversation about absent buyers from the lower farms, mentions of the Citadel and Maelor, and a refrain about wells gone dry and none returning from the Old Road. Beside her at the well stands a young smith's apprentice with a borrowed sword, who has halted and tilted his head to listen; with him is a figure of unremarkable appearance whose head is tilted slightly in the same listening posture, alongside another such figure. The apprentice later turns to face her and says, in a low cadence, "I tell Sera what I saw at the well this morning," while the unremarkable figure asks, "What did you see at the well." The square opens around her — broad cobbles, a ring of stone stalls heavy with unsold goods, the lane to the well at one side and the Old Road climbing away at the other. The apprentice moves to the center post and drives a plank of pale wood against an upright with three flat strikes; the plank holds. She stands two paces off and reads the uneven letters scratched across it: the account of what was seen at the village well that morning, a sealed mouth, a figure, a silence, and the closing of the Vale's wells by the hand at the Citadel. A short stub of charred wood and a cobbler's hammer hang at the apprentice's belt. The unremarkable figure at the well-end tells him, "Stay at the well. Where did that fall." Later she sees the apprentice, whom she now knows as Corin, standing beside the raised board at the center of the cobbles, the charcoal stick and cobbler's hammer set beside him. At the well-end, a figure of unremarkable appearance — Bryn — stands still, gaze steady on Corin; another such figure settles weight onto the flats of the feet, gaze passing between the board and Corin. The small press of bystanders thins; no one stops at the post. Corin later turns from the post, scanning the square for a rider heading east, two coins in his hand; the unremarkable figures ask, "Two coins. Where are you meaning to spend those." Sera answers that the coins are for the well at the lane below — a bucket and a dipper, not the road — and turns toward the lane with the coins in her near hand. From the well-end, Bryn holds position, gaze moving briefly from Corin to Sera's hands and back to the east passage she is watching; the other unremarkable figure rests gaze where Sera had been a moment before. Corin stands near the center of the square, watching the road end where the eastbound rider has already turned his bay pony toward the Old Road; the pony's hooves clatter across the cobbles and onto the packed dirt, and both rider and pony pass out of sight as the road curves eastward behind the hillside. Corin then crosses the cobbles toward the ring of trader carts and looks among the laden stalls for a salt master. Among the carts stand two heavy wagons loaded with coarse-sacked salt stacked head-high and lashed under oilcloth, bearing the painted brand of the Salt Road company (a white heap on a brown field) and a small bell at the yoke. A broad, sun-darkened man of middle years in a salt-stained leather coat and a wide-brimmed felt hat sits on the seat of the lead wagon with a coil of rope across his knees, watching the square unhurried. Corin asks him, "When do you next go east, and will you carry the same word at each stop along the way?" The unremarkable figure at the well-end mutters, "The same word as what." Corin steps up to the side of the heavy wagon and takes up a corner of the sacking over the nearest stack of salt, his hands moving with the rhythm of the loading. The salt master turns his head a fraction at the question but does not speak or stand. Sera stands still, coins loose in her near hand, her gaze on Corin and the wagon; Bryn stands beside her, still and unhurried, her gaze resting on the salt master's hands at the rope rather than on Corin's face. By the pale first light of a later morning, Corin lies asleep nearby with slow, steady breath. Sera and another figure of unremarkable appearance sit settled on the ground before her, their weight still, their gaze lifting once toward the lead salt wagon before resting back on the cobbles. The salt caravan master remains seated on the lead wagon with his coil of rope across his knees, watching silently. The square is quiet, the bell at the lead yoke unmoving, the rough plank nailed to the central post bearing its message, and the two heavy salt wagons stand among the ringed carts with their mules quiet in worn harness.

memory_summaries.summary: Wren stood at the dry village well in the morning quiet, alongside a young smith's apprentice carrying a borrowed sword and a still figure of unremarkable appearance whose gaze rested on the apprentice and the open passage to the market square. Fragments of conversation carried across the cobbles from the market square: talk of the Citadel, Maelor, the wells above having gone dry, and none returning from the Old Road. Wren moved into the market square, where the ring of stone stalls sat heavy with unsold goods and the Old Road climbed away at one edge of the cobbles. The apprentice lifted a pale plank against the center post and drove three flat strikes with a cobbler's hammer; the board held. The figure at the well-end asked the apprentice where something had fallen. Sera read a notice board — its face scratched over with uneven marks — and asked Corin directly whether the sealed mouth scratched on it was their well at the lane below or another, saying plainly that the next direction would follow from his answer. Corin produced two coins; the figure at the well-end asked where they were meant to be spent. Sera answered that the coins were for the well at the lane below — a bucket and a dipper, not the road — and turned toward the lane, coins held in her near hand. Wren and the figure of unremarkable appearance remained at the well-end, gazes settling where Sera had been. An eastbound rider turned his bay pony onto the Old Road and did not look back; the sound of hooves faded as the road curved eastward behind the hillside. Corin left the center post and crossed to the laden stalls, finding among the carts two heavy wagons of the Salt Road company, stacked head-high with coarse-sacked salt under oilcloth, branded with a white heap on a brown field and a small bell at the yoke. A broad, sun-darkened salt master in a salt-stained leather coat sat on the lead wagon's seat with a coil of rope across his knees, unhurried. Corin asked when the wagons next went east and whether they would carry the same word at each stop along the way, and took up a corner of sacking to work alongside the loading. Wren asked the salt master the same question in a mutter at the well-end. By the first pale light of the next morning, Corin lay asleep nearby; the salt master still sat on the lead wagon's seat with the coil of rope across his knees, the bell at the yoke still. Wren held position at the well-end, weight settled, gaze lifting once toward the lead salt wagon before resting back on the cobbles.

entries.content: The market square of the Vale is a wide, cobbled expanse ringed by low stone stalls and trader carts. In normal times it is the loudest place in the Vale — cattle, cloth, ironwork, bread. Lately the stalls stand full and the buyers do not come.
entries.title: The Market Square

entries.content: The Vale is a ring of villages and farms set about a central Citadel. Its people depend on a chain of wells and springs that have never, in living memory, run dry. Maelor the Ashen has begun sealing those wells one by one, and the higher villages have already gone thirsty.
entries.title: The Vale

entries.keys: Maelor the Ashen, Maelor, the Ashen
entries.content: Maelor, called the Ashen, holds the Citadel at the heart of the Vale. He is sealing the wells of the Vale one by one; his reason and his price are not yet known to the villages below. None have walked up the Old Road and come back to tell what he wants.
entries.title: Maelor the Ashen

entries.keys: Corin's notice, the notice on the post, notice at the central post, notice in the market square
entries.content: A roughly squared plank of pale wood nailed to the central post of the Vale market square, its face scratched over in uneven letters. It records the morning's happening at the well: the well's mouth was found sealed by a hand (not a tool), a figure stood nearby, and no sound was made — the wells are being closed by the hand at the Citadel. The well named on the board is the well at the lane below the square. Scribed by Corin and put up where the crowd in the square can read it.

entries.keys: morning's happening at the well, well-mouth sealed by hand, figure at the well, silence at the well, wells closed by the hand at the Citadel
entries.content: What Corin records having witnessed that morning at the well: the mouth of the well was sealed — by a hand, not a tool or stones; a figure stood nearby while it was done; no sound was made in the doing of it; and the cause is the hand at the Citadel, which is closing the wells of the Vale one by one.
entries.title: The morning's happening at the well (as recorded by Corin)

book.name: The Vale
book.summary: A ring of villages and farms set about a central Citadel, dependent on wells and springs that have begun to fail as Maelor the Ashen seals them.

book.name: Market Square
book.summary: The cobbled market square at the heart of the Vale, ringed by stalls and carts. Once the loudest place in the Vale, now full of goods with no buyers.

entries.keys: salt caravan, salt wagons, salt sacks at the square, Salt Road company, Salt Road brand, salt caravan master
entries.content: Two heavy wagons drawn up among the ringed carts of the market square, each loaded with coarse-sacked salt stacked head-high and lashed under oilcloth. The lead wagon bears the painted brand of the Salt Road company — a white heap on a brown field — and a bell hung from the yoke that has been stilled for the market. Mules, not horses, stand in the traces; the master sits on the lead wagon's seat, a broad, sun-darkened man of middle years in a salt-stained leather coat and a wide-brimmed felt hat, with a coil of rope across his knees.
entries.title: Salt caravan in the market square
